:::{#def-saddle-point}
#### Saddle point

Let $f : \reals^p \to \reals$.
A [stationary point](#def-stationary-point) of $f$ that is
neither a [local minimizer](algebra.qmd#def-local-minimizer)
nor a [local maximizer](#def-local-maximizer) of $f$
is a **saddle point** of $f$
[@wikipedia_saddle_point].

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-saddle-point}
#### A saddle point

Let $f(\vx) = x_1^2 - x_2^2$.
Its gradient is $\tp{(2 x_1,\ -2 x_2)}$, which is $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ only at $\vx = \vzero_{2 \times 1}$,
so $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ is a stationary point.
For every $t \ne 0$,

$$
\ba
f(t, 0)
&= t^2
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&> 0
&& \text{(} t \ne 0 \text{)}
\\
&= f(\vzero_{2 \times 1}),
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
f(0, t)
&= -t^2
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&< 0
&& \text{(} t \ne 0 \text{)}
\\
&= f(\vzero_{2 \times 1}).
&& \text{(substitute)}
\ea
$$

So every ball around $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ contains a point with a larger value of $f$ and a point with a smaller one.
Hence $\vzero_{2 \times 1}$ is neither a local minimizer nor a local maximizer,
and it is a saddle point.

:::
